title: ר' ישמעאל (סתם)

paragraphs: (a) Avot, chapters 3 and 4. In the Mishnah: Berakhot 7:3; Pe'ah 4:10; Demai 6:4; Kilayim 3:3, 6, 7; 6:4; Shevi'it 1:4; Terumot 4:5; Ma'aserot 3:5; Ḥallah 4:4; Shabbat 2:2, 15:3; Eruvin 1:2; Pesaḥim 10:9; Shekalim 3:2, 4:3–4; Yoma 4:1, 6:8; Sukkah 3:4; Ketubbot 5:8; Nedarim 3:11, 9:10; Nazir 6:3; Bava Batra 3:1, 6:4, 10:8; Sanhedrin 1:2; Shevuot 2:5, 3:5; Eduyot 2:4–6, 5:3; Avodah Zarah 1:2, 2:5, 4:1; Menaḥot 3:7, 10:1; Ḥullin 9:4; Bekhorot 3:1, 6:6, 12, 7:5; Arakhin 8:7; Keritot 2:5; Me'ilah 3:3; Kelim 2:2, 5:3, 7:3; Ohalot 3:5; Nega'im 1:2, 2:1, 8:9, 11:5, 12:3; Parah 1:3, 3:11, 8:11; Niddah 3:7, 6:12; Zavim 1:2; Mikva'ot 7:1, 8:3, 9:6; Yadayim 4:3; Tohorot 1:2; Uktzin 2:2.

(b) R. Akiva's colleague (and disputant). Tosafot writes that he is ben Elisha; see above, R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest, where I discussed this at length. Yuḥasin writes [in Seder HaDorot, under R. Yishmael ben Elisha]: Although Maimonides, chapter 2 of Eduyot and likewise in Madda, holds that R. Yishmael was R. Akiva's student and rules according to R. Yishmael, the ruling is true: in the first chapter of Shabbat, R. Ḥanina ruled like R. Yishmael. Although the law follows R. Akiva against his colleague, here R. Ḥanina ruled like R. Yishmael so that we should not think the law follows R. Akiva. But it seems to me that he was his colleague, rather than his student. Although at the end of Mo'ed Katan it relates that when his sons died four elders came to visit him—R. Tarfon, R. Elazar ben Azaryah, R. Yose HaGelili, and R. Akiva—and he said that he had troubled his teachers, this was courteous conduct. They themselves said that he was a great sage and expert in aggadah and that none should intrude upon his fellow's words. Had he been their student, they would not have had reason to be so apprehensive of him. Yuḥasin further writes [in Seder HaDorot, concerning the priests]: in chapter 5 of Zevaḥim (57a), R. Yishmael said, 'Go and tell R. Akiva: You erred'; so too at the end of Yoma (75b), he said, 'You erred.' If he were his teacher, how could he say this of him? Although Naḥmanides' Sha'ar HaGemul has the reading in Yoma that R. Akiva said to R. Yishmael, 'You erred,' this reading is not found in any copy. The aforementioned reading at the end of chapter Eizehu Mekoman also attests to this. Another proof that he was his colleague is that everywhere R. Yishmael's words precede R. Akiva's. Although we find R. Meir before R. Eliezer in two places, that is exceptional, rather than everywhere. In chapter Arba Mitot (51b), R. Akiva said to R. Yishmael, 'My brother.' R. Tarfon was like a teacher to R. Akiva (see his entry), while R. Elazar ben Azaryah put them on the same footing, calling R. Yishmael 'my brother,' first chapter of Berakhot (11a), Sanhedrin (51b), and R. Tarfon 'my brother,' chapter 4 of Yadayim. R. Yehoshua said, 'I am as one answering Tarfon, my brother.' In Bekhorot (20a), R. Yehoshua said, 'Go and tell R. Yishmael: You erred.' When R. Yose ben Durmaskit came to R. Elazar in Lod, he told him the incident (see his entry). Thus R. Yishmael's words were heard in the time of R. Akiva's teachers, R. Yehoshua and R. Tarfon. R. Eliezer likewise treated him as an equal, calling him 'my brother.' Ben Azzai, who was R. Akiva's student-colleague, also said, 'Alas that I did not attend R. Yishmael' (see his entry). At the end of Bava Batra (175), R. Yishmael said, 'One who wishes to become wise should engage in monetary law,' etc., and 'Anyone wishing to engage in monetary law should attend Shimon ben Nannas.' Although he praised ben Nannas, the law follows R. Yishmael. He called him 'ben Nannas,' without 'Rabbi'; ben Nannas is known to have been R. Akiva's colleague. In Sifra, R. Yishmael said to R. Eliezer, 'My teacher, it says,' etc.; R. Eliezer answered, 'You are a palm of the mountains.' It appears that he debated with R. Eliezer, R. Akiva's teacher. At the end of Yoma (86), R. Matya ben Ḥarash asked R. Elazar ben Azaryah: 'I heard of four divisions of atonement that R. Yishmael expounded.' In chapter 3 of Shevuot, R. Yoḥanan said: R. Yishmael attended ('Naḥum of Gam Zu, who expounded inclusions and exclusions'—a scribal error) R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah, who expounded generalizations and particulars, so he too expounded generalizations and particulars; R. Akiva attended Naḥum of Gam Zu, who expounded inclusions and exclusions, so he too expounded inclusions and exclusions. See above, R. Yishmael ben Elisha. If he were R. Akiva's student, why did he not expound like him? R.Ḥ. [ר״ח; provisionally Rabbenu Ḥananel] writes that R. Yishmael was R. Yehoshua's student, for he asked him about cheeses in Avodah Zarah (29b). This is also the reading in Rashi, Ḥullin (116b), and Midrash Ḥazit, at 'For your love is better.' But Ein Yaakov reads that R. Yishmael asked R. Akiva, and Responsa Rivash likewise reads that he asked R. Akiva, repeating this twice and three times; R. Yishmael there called R. Akiva 'my brother.' Ein Yaakov and Rivash's reading seems correct, for R. Yishmael called R. Akiva 'my brother,' and we likewise find R. Akiva calling R. Yishmael 'my brother'; we do not find in the Shas R. Yehoshua calling R. Yishmael 'my brother.' Yet Tosefta, Parah, chapter 9, says: R. Yishmael followed R. Yehoshua and asked, 'One pure for the sin-offering water moved the key'; he diverted him to another subject, saying, 'R. Yishmael, my brother, how do you read "For your love is better"?' etc. In Yalkut Shir HaShirim, at 'For your love is better,' it says R. Yehoshua asked R. Yishmael about those cheeses—certainly a scribal error. Tosafot, Avodah Zarah (35a), citing the Jerusalem Talmud (there, chapter 2, halakhah 8) and that Midrash Ḥazit, says R. Yishmael was young then. This appears to lend some support to identifying the child ransomed by R. Yehoshua as this R. Yishmael; see what I wrote under R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest. It appears here that R. Yishmael was young in R. Yehoshua's days. In chapter 6 of Kilayim, R. Yehoshua went to R. Yishmael at Kefar Aziz—another version: Ḥaziz—and he showed him his inherited vineyard. He and R. Akiva were called 'fathers of the world' (see his entry). He was called a well-stocked shop [חנות מזויינת; provisional reading], Gittin (67a).

(c) It was taught in R. Yishmael's school: the Torah is expounded by thirteen rules. The school of R. Yishmael taught, beginning of chapter Ḥelek. Tosafot, Pesaḥim (5a), notes that in several places they pose a contradiction between R. Yishmael and a teaching of R. Yishmael's school. In the first chapter of Yevamot (6b): R. Yishmael's school taught, 'You shall not kindle fire in any of your dwellings'—what does this teach? (Has it not already said, 'You shall do no labor'—Rashi.) It asks: what does it teach? According to R. Yose, kindling was singled out for a prohibition (to say that it incurs neither excision nor stoning, but only an ordinary prohibition); according to R. Natan, to distinguish the labors (lest you say that one incurs stoning only if one desecrates Shabbat through all the labors, etc.). In Tosafot, on 'Or is it not,' R. Yehudah Kohen asks: how could they seek to establish R. Yishmael according to R. Yose, who says kindling was singled out for a prohibition? In the first chapter of Shabbat (12), R. Yishmael read and tilted [the lamp], saying, 'When the Temple is rebuilt I shall bring a fat sin-offering.' Thus kindling incurs excision, as above. Tosafot thus poses a contradiction between a teaching of R. Yishmael's school and R. Yishmael. Similarly they pose a contradiction between a teaching of Levi's school and what Levi taught (see his entry). This also proves that R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague, is R. Yishmael ben Elisha: Tosafot objects that R. Yishmael read and tilted the lamp, while that passage says R. Yishmael ben Elisha read and tilted it. See above, R. Yishmael ben Elisha. If it were the High Priest, how could he say that when the Temple was rebuilt he would bring a sin-offering, since he was killed at the destruction? He made a Mekhilta from the book of Exodus to the Torah's end; R. Akiva likewise made a Mekhilta. I have seen R. Yishmael's Mekhilta from 'This month' to 'You shall not kindle fire.' Shalshelet HaKabbalah, folio 32b, writes that he composed the chapters of Heikhalot. This is an error: R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest composed it (see his entry). It also errs in saying that R. Yishmael, Rabbi's colleague—who is R. Yishmael son of R. Yose—composed the Mekhilta. This is not so; this R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague, composed it. Halikhot Olam's statement that undesignated Sifrei is R. Yishmael and that all follow R. Akiva's view because they were his students is erroneous, for R. Yishmael was not R. Akiva's student; this is explicit also in Temurah. Maimonides likewise writes in his responsa (see R. Shimon ben Yoḥai).

(d) 'It was taught in R. Yishmael's school': Shabbat (12, 26, 27, 35, 64, 98, 105, 114, 117, 151); Eruvin (19, 51); Pesaḥim (3, 5, 7, 35); Rosh HaShanah (16, 17); Ta'anit (6, 7, 8); Yoma (4, 28, 39, 44, 54, 58, 67, 81, 88); Sukkah (49, 52); Megillah (12, 25); Yevamot (4); Ketubbot (5, 33, 49, 72, 106); Kiddushin (20, 26, 29, 56); Gittin (6, 56, 59, 60, 66, 70); Nedarim (68); Sotah (3, 13, 36); Bava Kamma (64, 84); Bava Metzia (61, 111); Bava Batra (120); Avodah Zarah (11, 23); Sanhedrin (34, 35, 41, 42, 69, 73, 90, 91, 106, 108); Horayot (4, 7); Makkot (5, 19); Shevuot (9, 14, 47); Zevaḥim (12, 15, 24, 41, 88, 105); Ḥullin (42, 59, 65, 66, 67, 132, 137); Menaḥot (50, 66, 78); Bekhorot (5, 14); Arakhin (16); Keritot (22); Niddah (13); Bamidbar Rabbah (chapter 9); Shir HaShirim Rabbah, at 'My dove, in the clefts of the rock.'

(e) In the first chapter of Eruvin (13a): wherever it says that a student spoke in R. Yishmael's name before R. Akiva, it is R. Meir. A student spoke in R. Yishmael's name, first chapter of Yevamot (6b). In Sotah (20, end of side a): R. Meir studied before R. Akiva but did not understand because of the dialectical reasoning. He came and studied with R. Yishmael and mastered the received teaching, then returned to study reasoning with R. Akiva. In chapter 7 of Mikva'ot, R. Akiva said: R. Yishmael used to argue against me. Sefer Keritot [בם כריתות as printed; book reading provisional] writes that R. Elazar ben Shammua, R. Ḥananyah ben Teradyon, R. Yehudah, R. Yoḥanan the Sandalmaker, R. Yose, R. Neḥemyah, R. Shimon, and Shimon ben Azzai received from him. End of quotation. See above, R. Akiva: these are the ones R. Akiva established in his old age. It seems likely to me that they did not see R. Yishmael.

(f) Bava Kamma (80a): R. Yishmael said (another version: R. Shimon Shezuri), 'My father's house was among the householders of Upper Galilee. Why were they ruined? Because they grazed in the woodlands and adjudicated monetary cases alone.' In chapter 5 of Ketubbot, R. Yishmael allotted barley at twice the amount of wheat, since he was near Edom, where the barley was poor. At the end of chapter 9 of Nedarim (66a–b), and Tosefta, chapter 5: R. Yishmael used to sustain Israel's daughters during famine so that they would be beautiful (for one he made a gold tooth). In the Mishnah there, when he died Israel's daughters lamented him (and that eulogist): 'Daughters of Israel, weep for Yishmael,' as for Saul, 'who clothed you in scarlet with delights.' In the Jerusalem Talmud there: he sustained women whose husbands went to war, etc. In the other explanation, when he saw a group of colleagues, he gave them food and drink. When he heard a reason for a law from a sage, he praised him. His daughter came to refuse her marriage, with her son on her shoulder, Niddah (52a). In chapter 2 of Nega'im, he swore, 'May I be an atonement for the children of Israel.' Bekhorot (45): his students boiled a prostitute who had incurred death by burning from the king, and found 252 bodily members. His mother complained of him to his teachers: 'Rebuke Yishmael, my son, for he does not treat me with honor.' Their faces changed: could Yishmael ...? They asked her, 'What has he done to you?' She said, 'When he leaves the meeting house, I wish to wash his feet and drink from that water, and he does not let me.' They said to him: since this is her wish, it is her honor. Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah, chapter 1, halakhah 1, and Kiddushin, chapter 1, halakhah 7. שה״ק [title unresolved] writes this about R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest. He interpreted dreams for ben Dama, his sister's son, and for a Sadducee, and events occurred as he interpreted them, chapter HaRo'eh (56, end of side b). Yet in Jerusalem Talmud, Ma'aser Sheni, chapter 4, halakhah 9, and Eikhah Rabbah, at 'How she sits,' etc., 'great among the nations,' some of those Sadducees' dreams were put to R. Yishmael son of R. Yose. One who sees R. Yishmael in a dream should expect wisdom (see his entry, R. Yishmael the High Priest). Refadya is his burial place (see Naḥum of Gam Zu). R. Yishmael is Joseph's reincarnation (see above, R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest).

(g) In chapter Ḥezkat HaBattim (28a): R. Akiva says [concerning presumptive possession; the printed text has חזקיה], etc.; R. Yishmael says, etc. It says there: R. Yoḥanan said, 'I heard from those who went to Usha' (Rashbam explains: when the Sanhedrin was exiled from Yavneh to Usha), who said: whence [do we learn] that possession is established by three years? etc. There, side b: who are 'those who went to Usha' (in whose name R. Yoḥanan spoke)? R. Yishmael. Rashbam explains: this is their received tradition, that he lived at that time; see above, R. Yoḥanan. This seems to prove what I wrote under R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest: that R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague, was the High Priest's grandson and lived in the time of R. Yishmael son of R. Yose, who lived in Rabbi's time; R. Yoḥanan also lived in Rabbi's time. This is also necessary in light of what I wrote under Rabban Gamliel the Elder: those who went to Usha lived in the days of R. Shimon, Rabbi's father, contrary to the many who mistakenly held that they lived in Rabban Gamliel the Elder's time; see there at length [עשב״ג, provisional]. Yet it requires examination, for R. Yoḥanan was born when Rabbi was Nasi. In Eduyot, chapter 2, mishnah 4: R. Yishmael stated three things before the sages in the vineyard at Yavneh. Shir HaShirim Rabbah, at 'Solomon had a vineyard.' In chapter 3 of Sukkah: R. Yishmael, R. Tarfon, and R. Akiva. Tosafot, Sotah (4a): it is surprising that R. Yishmael's statement precedes those of R. Eliezer and R. Yehoshua.

(h) Yuḥasin writes [in Seder HaDorot, concerning the priests]: It appears that R. Yishmael was a priest (Maimonides did not mention him among the priests he listed). In chapter Ellu Terefot (49a), he disagrees with R. Akiva, giving a permissive ruling about stomach fat in his ancestors' name. They said, 'Yishmael the priest assists priests.' Rashi did not explain how he was a priest. Perhaps 'Yishmael the priest' is an allusion and comparison to R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest, one of the martyrs, etc. I found in some commentaries of Rashi to Ellu Terefot: 'He was a priest, and he is R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest.' This does not seem to accord with the Talmud: there are two, with a long interval between them, for the first was killed with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel before Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai assumed leadership. So too it appears in Tosafot, chapter Mitzvat Ḥalitzah: the martyr was the grandfather of the R. Yishmael ben Elisha whom R. Yishmael son of R. Yose saw. End of quotation. (See above, R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest, for a transcription of Tosafot's wording.)

(i) R. Ilai, R. Yehudah's father, was like his colleague (see his entry); he was his student. He sat with R. Elazar HaModa'i and R. Tarfon (see his entry). R. Elazar ben Azaryah (see above). R. Elazar ben Yitzḥak of Kefar Darom. R.A. [ר״א; provisionally R. Eliezer], his teacher. Abba Elazar ben Gamliel. R. Zekharyah, in his name. R. Ḥanina ben Antigonos, in his time. R. Yehoshua, his teacher. R. Ḥiyya bar Naḥmani, in his name. R. Yehoshua ben Matya explained the matters raised before him. R. Yehoshua ben Dama (see his entry). R. Yoḥanan heard from him (see above). R. Yoḥanan said in R. Yishmael's name [אר״י משום ר״י, provisional]. R. Yonatan. R. Yose ben HaḤotef, his student. Abba Yose ben Ḥanan. R. Yose HaGelili (see above). R. Yeynai, in R. Yishmael's name, in the name of R. Yeynai's house. R. Meir, his student (see above). R. Matya, in his name. R. Natan, in his name. R. Akiva, his colleague or teacher (see above). Shemuel, in his name. R. Shimon ben Nannas (see above). R. Shimon ben Yoḥai lived long after him.
